title: Alberta bill would ban some bike lanes, let transportation minister remove others
summary: Alberta’s government is proposing to ban future bike lanes that remove or restrict motor-vehicle traffic and give itself the power to remove some existing bike lanes.

image.caption: Bill 43 could allow bike lanes like this one, on Hermitage Road in northeast Edmonton, to be removed. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)

blocks.text: Alberta’s government is proposing to ban future bike lanes that remove or restrict motor-vehicle traffic and give itself the power to remove some existing bike lanes.
If passed, Bill 43 would raise fines for unsafe trucking operators, regulate personal e-scooters

Those changes are part of Bill 43, which the government is calling the Safe and Sensible Roads Act. It’s an omnibus bill that, in addition to bike lanes, seeks to increase penalties for unsafe commercial trucking operators, give the provincial government more oversight on municipal LRT projects and establish a framework and minimum safety standards for personal e-scooters and other similar devices.

According to a news release the government issued Thursday, the province will work with municipalities to ensure bike lanes are safely planned and fit within the broader transportation network. The proposed changes, the release said, would help make sure communities consider how bike lanes affect traffic flow, commuters, emergency services and the movement of goods.
Municipalities could request exemptions on a case-by-case basis, but must provide supporting information and rationale for the minister’s assessment, the release said.

items: Are people actually using Edmonton’s bike lanes? Here’s a look at the numbers

blocks.text: The proposed legislation does not include criteria municipalities must meet to qualify for exemptions, nor does it explain how bike lanes would be selected for removal and who would pay for removal costs.
If passed, the government expects the legislation would take effect in April, with regulations also scheduled to come in the spring.
Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen has been saying for months that bike lanes make sense in some locations, but should not take away parking spaces or traffic lanes used by motor vehicles.

items: Alberta’s government asked residents to complain about bike lanes. Here’s what rolled in.

blocks.text: Some residents agree with the minister and have expressed their concerns about specific bike lanes with him. Bike lane supporters and urban planning experts have said bike lanes make roads safer for everyone and help reduce traffic.

Dreeshen told CBC News in August he was emboldened by the Ontario Court of Appeal, which overturned a lower court’s decision that the Ontario government’s plan to replace some bike lanes with car lanes was unconstitutional.

Alberta’s Safe and Sensible Roads Act, if passed by the Legislature, would also allow municipalities to authorize privately-owned and rented e-scooters — and other personal micromobility devices — and create rules for them that meet or exceed provincial minimum safety standards.
Currently, citizens in Calgary and Edmonton can ride e-scooters from companies like Lime, but Albertans can’t legally ride their own devices without exemptions from the province.

items: Alberta gov't mulling regulations around micromobility vehicles like e-scooters

blocks.text: The government also intends to change the name of the Public Transit and Green Infrastructure Project Act to the Urban Rail Transit Act.
This new act would apply to current and future urban rail transit lines and make municipalities tell the provincial cabinet minister about planned changes to them.
The government says these changes would expand provincial oversight and ensure cities’ LRT projects align with provincial priorities.
